name: Massachusetts

sales.rateNote: 6.25% state sales and use tax on tangible personal property and telecommunications services. There is no general local sales tax; cities and towns may add a 0.75% local option meals excise on restaurant meals.

local.levies: no local general sales tax; cities and towns may adopt a local option meals excise (0.75%) and a local room occupancy excise
local.capNote: Local option meals excise: 0.75% on top of the 6.25% sales tax on meals (7% total).

groceries.note: Food for human consumption is exempt (other than meals sold by restaurants, which are taxable including take-out). Baked goods sold in units of 6 or more for take-out and vending snacks under $3.50 are exempt; vitamins and dietary supplements are taxable.

clothing.note: Clothing and footwear are exempt up to $175 per item; above that, tax applies only to the amount over $175 (a $200 suit pays $1.56). Athletic or protective gear, handbags, jewelry and accessories are taxable.

otherRates.note: Plus 0.75% local option meals excise where adopted.
The buyer pays the tax directly to the Commonwealth (Form RTA) within 10 days of purchase, not to the dealer.

holidays2026.name: Massachusetts Sales Tax Holiday
holidays2026.items: most retail items of $2,500 or less bought for personal use; excludes meals, motor vehicles, motorboats, telecom, utilities, tobacco, marijuana and alcohol

useTax.note: 6.25% on items used in Massachusetts on which no (or less) sales tax was paid; individuals report it on Form 1 (with an optional 'safe harbor' estimate for items under $1,000) or Form ST-11, due April 15.

facts.text: Clothing is tax-free up to $175 per item; above that only the excess is taxed, so a $200 suit carries $1.56 of tax.
The 2026 sales tax holiday was Saturday August 8 and Sunday August 9: items up to $2,500 each were tax-free for personal use.
During the holiday, an item costing more than $2,500 is taxed on its full price, not just the excess.
Restaurant meals cost 7% in towns that adopted the 0.75% local option meals excise.
Digital music, video and e-books are not taxed when delivered electronically, but software and remote software access are.
Residential electricity, gas and heating fuel are exempt, as is local residential phone service up to $30 a month.
Remote sellers must register once their Massachusetts sales exceed $100,000 in a calendar year.

property.levied: cities and towns only (local property tax); the Department of Revenue's Division of Local Services certifies assessments and enforces Proposition 2½

assessment.text: Local assessors must value all property at its full and fair cash value as of January 1 and classify it as residential, open space, commercial or industrial; communities may shift part of the tax burden from residential to commercial, industrial and personal property. DOR reviews each community's assessments every five years. Proposition 2½ (G.L. c. 59, s. 21C) limits each community's total levy; overrides and exclusions require voter approval.

homestead.name: No statewide homestead exemption
homestead.text: Massachusetts has no statewide homestead exemption. Relief comes from local exemptions under G.L. c. 59, s. 5 (seniors, surviving spouses, veterans, blind persons) granted by local assessors, and from the state Senior Circuit Breaker income tax credit.
homestead.applyBy: Exemptions: apply to the local assessors.

otherRelief.name: Senior Circuit Breaker Tax Credit
otherRelief.text: Refundable income tax credit for homeowners and renters 65+ whose property tax (plus half of water/sewer) exceeds 10% of income; maximum $2,820 for tax year 2025; income limits $75,000 single, $94,000 head of household, $112,000 joint; home assessed at no more than $1,298,000.

otherRelief.name: Local exemptions (G.L. c. 59, s. 5)
otherRelief.text: Exemptions for blind persons, qualifying seniors, surviving spouses, minor children and elderly persons, and veterans, filed with local assessors.

facts.text: Seniors can get up to $2,820 back on their income tax (2025) when property tax exceeds 10% of their income.
Since 1978, cities and towns may tax residential property at a lower rate than commercial and industrial property (classification).
The Department of Revenue certifies each community's property values every five years.
Proposition 2½ limits how much property tax a town can raise in total; going above requires an override or exclusion vote.
Since November 1, 2024, an owner whose home is foreclosed for unpaid taxes is entitled to the excess equity from the sale.
